questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how two restrictions combine
questions.stem: The translator's notes ask for an explanation of how two restrictions combine to give a domain. Write your answer for the glossary.

answer.exemplar: A domain records the inputs for which every part of a rule makes sense, and a rule with two restrictions has to satisfy both of them at once, so the domain is the set of inputs that pass both tests rather than the union of the sets that pass one. Take the rule 1 divided by the quantity x minus 4, plus the square root of x minus 1. The denominator gives the restriction that x cannot be 4, and the root gives the restriction that x minus 1 must be zero or more, that is x at least 1. Writing the two together gives every input from 1 upwards with 4 cut out of it, and the boundary at 1 is kept because the square root of zero is a real number. The useful habit is to state each restriction separately first and then intersect them, since an input can fail either one.

questions.explanation: Two restrictions must hold at the same time, so the domain is the intersection of the two sets of allowed inputs, and the boundary of a root is kept.
questions.hint: Find each restriction, then keep only the inputs passing both.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how a step value is read
questions.stem: A glossary entry in the translator's notes asks for an explanation of how a value is read from a step rule. Write your answer for the glossary.

answer.exemplar: A step rule is written as a list of bands, each with a condition and a value, and reading it means testing the input against each condition until one holds, then taking the value attached to that band. Take the printing price of 3 for fewer than 50 pages, 5 for 50 pages up to 199, and 8 for 200 pages or more. A document of 150 pages is not fewer than 50 and is not 200 or more, so it lands in the middle band and costs 5. The boundary wording matters too, since a band that runs up to 199 pages includes 199, and a band that starts at 200 pages includes 200. The whole point of a step rule is that the value stays flat inside a band, so no interpolation or averaging is appropriate anywhere.

questions.explanation: To read a step rule, test the input against each band condition in turn and take the value of the first band that holds, because the value is flat inside a band.
questions.hint: Find the band whose condition the input satisfies.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Minimum of an absolute value function
questions.learningObjective: explain how the smallest value is found
questions.stem: The glossary draft asks for an explanation of how the smallest value of an absolute value rule is found. Write your answer for the glossary.

answer.exemplar: The smallest value of a rule built on an absolute value is found by making the absolute value as small as it can be, which is zero, and then evaluating the rest of the rule at that input. An absolute value is never negative, so the quantity inside the bars can only push the result up, and it equals zero exactly when the input makes the expression inside the bars equal to zero. Take the rule 2 times the absolute value of x plus 1, then minus 3: the inside is zero at x equals negative 1, so the smallest value is 2 times 0 minus 3, which is negative 3. The same input is also the turning point of the graph, and the two facts are often confused, since the lowest point of a graph is a height while the turn is a location.

questions.explanation: The smallest value comes from making the absolute value term zero, at one input, and then evaluating the whole rule there. The turn of the graph and its lowest height differ.
questions.hint: Set the quantity inside the bars to zero, then evaluate.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how a piecewise rule is evaluated
questions.stem: A glossary entry asks for an explanation of how a piecewise rule is evaluated at a given input. Write your answer for the glossary.

answer.exemplar: A piecewise rule is a list of rules each with its own condition, and evaluating it at a given input means finding the condition that input satisfies and then using only the rule attached to that condition. Take the rule 2x plus 1 for inputs below 3, and x squared minus 2 for inputs of 3 or more, evaluated at the input 4. The input 4 is not below 3, so the first condition fails and the second one holds, and the second rule gives 4 squared minus 2, which is 14. The wording of the conditions carries the boundary, so at the input 3 it is the second rule that applies, and the first rule would have given 7. Testing the condition before doing any arithmetic is the habit that prevents the common slip of using whichever rule is written first.

questions.explanation: Evaluate a piecewise rule by testing the input against the conditions and using only the rule whose condition holds, so the boundary wording decides the case at 3.
questions.hint: Test the conditions before doing any arithmetic.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how an inverse rule is built
questions.stem: A glossary request in the translator's notes asks for an explanation of how an inverse rule is built by switching roles.

answer.exemplar: An inverse rule runs a rule backwards, and the way to build one is to write the original with y standing for the output, exchange the letters so that x stands for the output and y for the input, and then solve for y. Take the rule f of x equals 3x minus 6. Writing y equals 3x minus 6 and swapping the letters gives x equals 3y minus 6, and solving that for y gives y equal to the quantity x plus 6 divided by 3. The result is checked by composing the two rules in either order and confirming that the original input comes back, which is the only reliable test that the reversal was done correctly. A quick warning sign is a rule that still multiplies by 3, since a genuine inverse of a rule that scales by 3 must scale by one third.

questions.explanation: An inverse is built by writing the rule with y for the output, exchanging the letters, and solving for y, and it is checked by feeding the result back in.
questions.hint: Swap the letters, then solve for the old input.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain why a root boundary is included
questions.stem: A boundary note in the translator's file asks for an explanation of why the boundary of a square root rule is allowed.

answer.exemplar: The boundary of a square root rule is allowed because the square root of zero is itself a real number, and the condition that a root imposes is that the quantity inside it is zero or more, not that it is greater than zero. Take the rule the square root of x minus 4: the radicand is zero at the input 4, and the value of the rule there is 0, which is a perfectly ordinary output, so the input 4 belongs to the domain and the domain is every input from 4 upwards. This is different from a denominator, where the boundary is excluded because division by zero is undefined, so the two kinds of boundary must not be confused with one another. In the notes it is worth stating each condition as zero or more whenever a root is present, since that wording removes the ambiguity at once.

questions.explanation: A square root accepts zero, so the boundary of a root is included, unlike the boundary of a denominator, where division by zero is undefined.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.learningObjective: explain how a composition domain is found
questions.stem: A composition note in the translator's notes asks for an explanation of how the domain of a composition is found. Write your answer for the glossary.

answer.exemplar: The domain of a composition is the set of inputs for which the inner rule produces a value that the outer rule accepts, and the easiest way to find it is to write the composition as a single rule and then read off its restrictions. Take f of x equals the square root of x and g of x equals 2x minus 10. Substituting gives the square root of the quantity 2x minus 10, and the restriction is that 2x minus 10 must be zero or more, which gives the inputs from 5 upwards, with 5 included. The same answer comes from asking what the inner rule produces and comparing that with the domain of the outer rule, and the two methods agree whenever they are applied correctly. A common mistake is to use the domain of the outer rule on its own, which admits inputs that the inner rule sends to values the outer rule cannot accept.

questions.explanation: The domain of a composition is the set of inputs where the inner rule's output is acceptable to the outer rule, and writing the composition as one rule makes that visible.
questions.hint: Write the composition as a single rule first.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Deciding a table defines a function
questions.learningObjective: explain how to test a table of terms
questions.stem: A glossary explanation in the translator's notes asks for an explanation of how to decide whether a table of terms and renderings defines a function.

answer.exemplar: A table of terms and renderings defines a function when every term in the input column is paired with exactly one rendering in the output column, and the test is made by scanning the input column for a term that appears more than once and then comparing the renderings written beside it. If the repeated term always carries the same rendering, the table is a function, because nothing is ambiguous. If it carries two different renderings, then that one term would need two outputs, and the table is a relation rather than a function. The point that causes most confusion is the opposite one: two different terms sharing the same rendering is perfectly acceptable, since a function restricts how many outputs one input may have and says nothing about how many inputs may share an output. A table like this is therefore often a function even when it has fewer renderings than terms.

questions.explanation: A table defines a function when each input carries exactly one output, and the check is to scan the input column for repeated entries and compare them.
questions.hint: Scan the inputs, then compare the entries beside repeats.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_I
questions.topic: Finding a domain from two restrictions
questions.learningObjective: explain how a domain is found from two restrictions
questions.stem: A domain request in the translator's notes asks for an explanation of how a domain is found when a rule carries two restrictions.

answer.exemplar: A domain is found by listing every input for which each part of a rule makes sense, so a rule with two restrictions is handled by writing each restriction down on its own and then keeping the inputs that satisfy both of them at once. Take the rule the quantity x minus 2 divided by the square root of x minus 1. The denominator gives the restriction that x cannot be 2, and the root gives the restriction that x minus 1 must be zero or more, that is x at least 1. Combining them gives every input from 1 upwards with 2 cut out of it, and the boundary 1 is kept because the square root of zero is a real number. The habit worth keeping is to state each restriction separately first, because an input can fail either one, and writing the domain from a single restriction is the usual source of error.

questions.explanation: Each restriction is found on its own and then the two are combined, keeping only the inputs that satisfy both, with the boundary of a root allowed.
questions.hint: State each restriction first, then keep the inputs passing both.

answer.exemplar: The domain of a composition is the set of inputs whose outputs are accepted by the outer rule, so it is found by comparing the range of the inner rule with the domain of the outer one, and it can never be larger than the domain of the inner rule. Take an inner rule that produces values from 1 to 6 and an outer rule that accepts inputs from 4 upwards. The values 4, 5 and 6 are accepted and the values 1, 2 and 3 are not, so the composition loses exactly the inputs whose outputs fell short, and the two sets of figures make that visible at once. The same comparison can be made in the other direction, by asking which inputs of the inner rule could produce an accepted output, and the two answers agree. Saying that both rules are defined everywhere does not settle the question, because the issue is what one rule hands to the other.

questions.explanation: The domain of a composition is found by comparing the inner range with the outer domain, and it can never exceed the inner rule's own domain.
questions.hint: Compare the two sets rather than the rules alone.
